visuals.heading: Why Engineers Already Have a Head Start

items.text: Roughly 60-70% of product managers come from engineering or technical backgrounds, so you are not fighting the odds by trying.

blocks.heading: Nobody Has Made You a PM Yet

items.text: This is the step most engineers skip, and it is the single biggest reason technically strong candidates get passed over.

Find a feature, bug backlog, or small internal tool nobody owns and run its full lifecycle: talk to the people who will use it, write a one-page problem statement, get it built (even if you build it yourself), and track what changed after it shipped.
Document the problem, the options you considered, why you picked one, and the measurable result.
Before you spend months building toward this switch, run yourself through the same four-part check that applies to any real career decision: your fit, your situation, the job market and AI-proofing.
Do you get energy from ambiguous, people-heavy problems with no clean right answer, or do you get drained by them.
If what you actually dislike is your current company or manager, not the nature of engineering work itself, a PM switch will not fix that.

figures.label: Estimated Time Required
figures.source: An internal transfer, once you start visibly taking on product-shaped work, commonly takes about 6-9 months of deliberate positioning before a real opening or a real conversation with your manager lands. An external switch, including proof-of-work building and a genuine job search, more commonly runs 6-18 months, longer if you are also completing an MBA or making a full industry change at the same time.

visuals.heading: Resume and Linkedin for the Switch

items.text: Rewrite your strongest project bullets around impact and decisions, not implementation: "Prioritized X over Y after user data showed Z, resulting in [measurable change]" beats "Built X using React and Node."

Pull out every moment you already influenced a decision without being the manager, a design call, a scope cut, a prioritization argument you won, and put it front and center, even if it happened informally.

Your LinkedIn headline should state the direction plainly (for example, "Software Engineer moving into Product Management" or "Engineer building product management case studies") rather than only listing your current job title.
Add your case study or side project as a visible link on your profile and resume, not something you only mention if asked.
